facts.text: With the signing of the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso, Spain returned the colonial territory of Louisiana to France in return for territories in the Italian region of Tuscany.
St Pancras railway station in London, now the terminus of the Channel Tunnel Rail Link, opened to the public.
In boxing, Muhammad Ali defeated Joe Frazier in a match known as the " Thrilla in Manila ".
Civil unions between same-sex couples were legalised in Denmark, the first country to do so.
The International Court of Justice ruled that Chile was under no obligation to restore Bolivia's access to the Pacific Ocean, which it had lost in the 19th century.

links.title: Obligation to Negotiate Access to the Pacific Ocean

facts.text: Edgar acceded to the English throne upon the death of his brother Eadwig.
The Wonderful Parliament met at Westminster Abbey to address King Richard II 's need for money, but soon changed focus to the reform of his administration.
The first political gathering of colonists in Mexican Texas convened to seek reforms from the Mexican government.
At the encouragement of preservationist John Muir and writer Robert Underwood Johnson, the U.S. Congress established Yosemite National Park in California.
First World War: British and Arab troops captured Damascus from the Ottoman Empire.
Chinese Communist Party chairman Mao Zedong publicly proclaimed the establishment of the People's Republic of China in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

image.caption: Anthem: 义勇军进行曲 Yìyǒngjūn jìnxíngqǔ " March of the Volunteers "

links.title: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China

facts.text: The Free Speech Movement was launched at the University of California, Berkeley, when a crowd of 3,000 students prevented police from transporting Jack Weinberg away after his arrest.

Seven Indonesian National Armed Forces officers, six of them generals, were murdered at dawn by a rebellious force in Jakarta; the Army then blamed the Communist Party, leading to a mass anti-communist purge that killed up to one million people.
Fifty Rwandan Patriotic Front rebels deserted their Ugandan Army posts and crossed the border from Uganda into Rwanda, marking the start of the Rwandan Civil War.
A tribunal was established to consider matters relating to the constitution of Singapore upon referral by the president.

links.title: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore Tribunal

facts.text: Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, was formed with the ratification of the Europol Convention by all member states.
A levy was imposed on the hiring of foreign domestic helpers in Hong Kong, who numbered in the hundreds of thousands at the time.

links.title: Foreign domestic helpers in Hong Kong

facts.text: A ferry collision off Lamma Island, Hong Kong, killed 39 people and injured 92 others.
A lone gunman fired more than 1,000 rounds of ammunition from his hotel suite on a crowd attending the Route 91 Harvest music festival on the Las Vegas Strip, resulting in 60 deaths and 867 injuries.
Stanford University, founded by railroad magnate and politician Leland Stanford and his wife Jane in Palo Alto, California, admitted its first students.

image.caption: Motto Die Luft der Freiheit weht ( German ) [ 1 ]

facts.text: A deputation of Muslim leaders led by the Aga Khan III met Indian viceroy Lord Minto to secure greater political representation, eventually leading to the founding of the All-India Muslim League.
Mensa, the largest and oldest high- IQ society in the world, was formed in the United Kingdom.
Croatian War of Independence: Yugoslav People's Army forces invaded the area surrounding Dubrovnik, Croatia, beginning a seven-month siege of the city.
After losing a league home match to local rivals Persebaya Surabaya, some 3,000 Arema supporters invaded the stadium 's pitch and met with police resistance, causing a stampede that killed 135.
With King Edward IV of England forced to flee to the Burgundian Netherlands after a rebellion organised by Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick, Henry VI was restored to the throne.

Mexican dragoons dispatched to disarm settlers at Gonzales in Mexican Texas encountered stiff resistance from a Texian militia at the Battle of Gonzales, the first armed engagement of the Texas Revolution.
Second World War: HMS Curacoa was accidentally rammed and sunk by RMS Queen Mary while escorting the liner to provide protection from submarine attacks.
A hijacked airliner collided with two other planes while attempting to land at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport in China, killing 128 and injuring 71.
The Washington Post journalist Jamal Khashoggi was assassinated in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, Turkey.
Thurgood Marshall was sworn in as the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States

facts.text: Typhoon Longwang made landfall in China as the deadliest tropical cyclone in that year to impact the country.
As part of wider food riots, citizens in Nottingham, England, looted large quantities of cheese; one man was killed during attempts to restore order.
Qing China signed the Treaty of Livadia with the Russian Empire, but the terms were so unfavorable that the Chinese government refused to ratify the treaty.
The Shubert Theatre opened on Broadway with a production of Hamlet.
Nguyễn Văn Thiệu was re-elected unopposed as President of South Vietnam.
A gunman killed five Amish girls before committing suicide in a one-room schoolhouse in Nickel Mines, Pennsylvania.
Muhammad VII became the twelfth sultan of the Emirate of Granada.
Anglo-Spanish War: An English fleet intercepted and attacked six Spanish ships at the Battle of the Narrow Seas.

image.caption: Date 3–4 October 1602 Location Strait of Dover in the English Channel 51°00′N 1°27′E ﻿ / ﻿ 51.000°N 1.450°E ﻿ / 51.000; 1.450 Result Anglo-Dutch victory [ 1 ] [ 2 ]

facts.text: American author Edgar Allan Poe was found semi-conscious and delirious in Baltimore under mysterious circumstances; it was the last time he was seen in public before his death four days later.
The United Kingdom successfully conducted its first nuclear test, becoming the world's third state with nuclear weapons.

links.title: List of states with nuclear weapons

facts.text: Nadine Gordimer became the first South African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
In Major League Baseball, the New York Giants ' Bobby Thomson hit the " Shot Heard 'Round the World ", a game-winning home run, to win the National League pennant.

links.title: List of National League pennant winners

facts.text: The First Battle of Maryang-san, widely regarded as one of the Australian Army 's greatest accomplishments during the Korean War, began.
Mercury-Atlas 8, the fifth United States crewed space mission, was launched from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida, carrying astronaut Wally Schirra.
A hunger strike by Irish republican prisoners at HM Prison Maze outside Belfast, Northern Ireland, ended after seven months and ten deaths.
Major Moisés Giroldi of the Panama Defense Forces failed in his attempt to overthrow dictator Manuel Noriega.
The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008, establishing the Troubled Asset Relief Program, commonly referred to as a bailout of the U.S. financial system, was enacted.
A boat carrying migrants from Libya to Italy sank off the Italian island of Lampedusa, resulting in more than 360 deaths.
Spanish forces departed Valdivia to suppress the indigenous Huilliche uprising in southern Chile.
Vancouver's Holy Rosary Cathedral was dedicated by Archbishop William Mark Duke, fifty-three years after it first opened.
Oswaldo López Arellano replaced Honduran president Ramón Villeda Morales in a violent coup, initiating two decades of military rule.
Sinéad O'Connor tore up a photograph of Pope John Paul II on live television.

links.title: Sinéad O'Connor on Saturday Night Live

facts.text: Roy Horn of the American entertainment duo Siegfried & Roy was mauled by a tiger during a performance at the Mirage on the Las Vegas Strip.

image.caption: Other names Masters of the Impossible SARMOTI (Siegfried & Roy Masters of the Impossible) [ 1 ]

facts.text: Red Turban Rebellions: The rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang won the Battle of Lake Poyang by deploying ships intentionally set aflame when the emperor tried to escape.
Texas A&M University opened as the first public institution of higher education in the U.S. state.
First World War: The Allies devastated the German defence at the Battle of Broodseinde, prompting a crisis among German commanders and causing a severe loss of morale in the 4th Army.
First World War: The Japanese merhant ship Hirano Maru was sunk by a German submarine in the Celtic Sea with the loss of 291 lives.
Willie Gillis, one of Norman Rockwell 's trademark characters, debuted on the cover of The Saturday Evening Post.
World War II: Allied forces executed Operation Leader, an air raid against German shipping near Bodø, Norway.
Skanderbeg and Gjergj Arianiti signed a peace treaty to end the Albanian–Venetian War.
Smolensk War: Forces from the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth broke the Russian siege of Smolensk (depicted).
American Civil War: After a naval battle in Galveston Harbor, Texas, Confederate commanders negotiated the surrender of the city to Union forces.
Great Syrian Revolt: Rebels led by Fawzi al-Qawuqji captured the city of Hama from the French Mandate of Syria.

links.title: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon

facts.text: Gutzon Borglum and approximately 400 workers began sculpting Mount Rushmore.
The Fourth Council of Constantinople, the eighth Catholic Ecumenical Council, was convened to discuss the patriarchate of Photios I of Constantinople.
French Revolution: Upset about the high price and scarcity of bread, thousands of Parisian women and allies marched on the Palace of Versailles.
During construction of the Eastman tunnel in St. Anthony, Minnesota (now Minneapolis ), the Mississippi River broke through the tunnel's limestone ceiling, nearly destroying Saint Anthony Falls.
Around 200 men began a 291-mile (468 km) march from Jarrow to London, carrying a petition to the British government requesting the re-establishment of industry in the town.
" Love Me Do ", the first single by the Beatles, was released in the United Kingdom.
The U.S. suspended the Commercial Import Program, its main economic support for South Vietnam, in response to the oppression of Buddhists by President Ngô Đình Diệm.

Eugene Hasenfus 's plane was shot down by Nicaraguan forces while carrying weapons to the Contra rebels on behalf of the U.S. government; he was subsequently captured, leading to an international controversy.
During the United States vice-presidential debate, Democratic candidate Lloyd Bentsen told his opponent Dan Quayle, " Senator, you're no Jack Kennedy."
Swiss police found the bodies of 48 members of the Order of the Solar Temple, who had died in a cult mass murder-suicide.

Two trains collided head-on in Ladbroke Grove, London, killing 31 people, injuring 417, and severely damaging public confidence in the management and regulation of safety of Britain's privatised railway system.
Two Chinese cargo ships were attacked and their crews murdered on a stretch of the Mekong River in far northern Thailand.
A Cherokee band attacked settlers near Larissa, Texas, killing or abducting 18 people.
Samuel Griffith became the first Chief Justice of Australia, while Edmund Barton and Richard O'Connor became the first Puisne Justices of the High Court of Australia.

links.title: List of justices of the High Court of Australia

facts.text: Dr. No, the first James Bond film, was released.

Colour revolutions: During protests over irregularities in the Yugoslavian general election, a wheel-loader was driven into the Radio Television of Serbia building, giving the protests the nickname " Bulldozer Revolution ".
Formula One racing driver Jules Bianchi sustained fatal head injuries in a crash at the Japanese Grand Prix, dying the following year.
Transition from Sui to Tang: Wang Shichong 's army defeated Li Mi 's forces at the Battle of Yanshi, allowing Wang to consolidate power and soon depose China's Sui dynasty.
Austria-Hungary announced the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, causing a crisis that permanently damaged the country's relations with the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Serbia.

links.title: Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina

facts.text: The Jazz Singer, one of the first feature-length motion pictures with a synchronized recorded music score, was released.

Catalonia 's autonomous government, led by Lluís Companys, declared a general strike, an armed insurgency, and the establishment of the Catalan State in reaction to the inclusion of conservatives in the Spanish republican regime.

image.caption: Date 5-10 October 1934 Location Catalonia Result Spanish government victory

facts.text: The Egyptian Armed Forces crossed the Suez Canal to attack occupying Israeli forces at the Bar Lev Line in the Sinai Peninsula, beginning the Yom Kippur War.

image.caption: Date 6–8 October 1973 Location Sinai Peninsula , Egypt Result Egyptian victory [ 1 ] Territorial changes The Suez Canal comes under Egyptian control Fall of Israel's Bar-Lev Line

facts.text: Two bombs placed by the CIA-linked Cuban dissident group Coordination of United Revolutionary Organizations exploded on Cubana Flight 455, killing all 73 people aboard.
Egyptian president Anwar Sadat was assassinated while attending a parade in Cairo to mark the eighth anniversary of the Crossing of the Bar Lev Line at the start of the 1973 Arab-Israeli War.
About 200 members of the San Francisco Police Department instigated a police riot in the Castro following a peaceful protest held by the political group ACT UP.
Matthew Shepard, a gay college student, was attacked and fatally wounded near Laramie, Wyoming, U.S., dying six days later.
Al-Qaeda bombed the oil tanker Limburg, causing oil to leak into the Gulf of Aden.
The MESSENGER probe discovered Mercury's Rembrandt – the second largest impact crater on the planet.
Seven Years' War: The Battle of Manila concluded with a British victory over Spain, leading to a twenty-month occupation.
American Revolutionary War: Fort Clinton and Fort Montgomery were captured by British forces under Sir Henry Clinton, dismantling the Hudson River Chains.

links.title: Battle of Forts Clinton and Montgomery

facts.text: Police constable Keith Blakelock was killed during rioting in the Broadwater Farm housing estate in Tottenham, London.
Astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz reported the discovery of a planet orbiting 51 Pegasi (depicted) as the first known exoplanet around a main-sequence star.
Denouncing corruption in Argentine president Fernando de la Rúa 's administration and the Senate, Vice President Carlos Álvarez resigned.
King George III issued a royal proclamation that forbade British settlement of much of newly acquired French territory in North America, reserving the land for indigenous peoples.

American writer Edgar Allan Poe died under mysterious circumstances at Washington Medical College four days after being found on the streets of Baltimore, Maryland, in a delirious and incoherent state.
Japan captured Pohnpei from Germany, eventually leading to large-scale Japanese immigration to Micronesia.

The Holocaust: Sonderkommando work-unit members in Auschwitz concentration camp revolted upon learning that they were due to be killed; although a few managed to escape, most were massacred on the same day.
Anna Politkovskaya, a Russian journalist and human-rights activist, was assassinated in the elevator of her apartment block in Moscow.
Ottoman–Habsburg wars: The Battle of Lepanto was fought near the Gulf of Corinth, a significant setback for the Ottoman Empire and the last major naval battle fought entirely with galleys.
The French privateer Robert Surcouf led a 150-man crew to capture the 40-gun, 437-man East Indiaman Kent.
William II became King of the Netherlands after his father William I abdicated the throne.
Ōdate, the last castle of the Satake clan in Japan's Tōhoku region, was captured during the Boshin War.

The state funeral of Mindon Min, who ruled Myanmar for 25 years, took place; his death was reportedly preceded by strange omens, and his senior princes were unable to attend as they had all been arrested.

image.caption: Date 1 October 1878 (date of death) 7 October 1878 (date of ceremonial funeral)

links.title: Death and state funeral of Mindon Min

facts.text: Georgia Tech defeated Cumberland University 222–0 in the most lopsided college football game in American history.

links.title: 1916 Cumberland vs. Georgia Tech football game

facts.text: Near Point Barrow in Alaska, an Iñupiat hunter discovered three gray whales trapped in pack ice, which resulted in an international effort to free them.
Croatian War of Independence: The Yugoslav People's Army conducted an air strike on Banski Dvori, the official residence of the president of Croatia in Zagreb.
2008 TC 3 exploded above the Nubian Desert in Sudan, in the first time that an asteroid impact had been predicted prior to atmospheric entry.
Palestinian nationalist groups launched armed incursions into the Gaza envelope, starting the Gaza war.
War of the League of Cambrai: A Venetian army under Bartolomeo d'Alviano was decisively defeated by the Spanish army commanded by Ramón de Cardona and Fernando d'Ávalos.

links.title: War of the League of Cambrai

facts.text: American Revolutionary War: Patriots and Loyalist militias engaged each other at the Battle of Kings Mountain in South Carolina.
Seven-year-old Theo Faiss dies in an accident that Rudolf Steiner terms a voluntary sacrifice, and that inspires Edith Maryon 's relief In Memory of Theo Faiss.
During severe floods in Puerto Rico, about 130 people died as a result of the deadliest single landslide on record in North America.
The military wing of the Palestinian nationalist Islamist political organization Hamas massacred people attending an open-air music festival in southern Israel.
The Council of Chalcedon, a Christian ecumenical council, opened, and went on to repudiate the Eutychian doctrine of monophysitism and set forth the Chalcedonian Creed.
The Great Chicago Fire, began and proceeded to destroy much of the city's central business district, killing 300 people and leaving 90,000 others homeless.

World War I: After his platoon suffered heavy casualties during the Meuse–Argonne offensive in France's Forest of Argonne, American Corporal Alvin York led the 7 remaining men on an attack against a German machine gun nest; 25 German soldiers were killed and 132 captured.
The Indian Air Force was founded as an auxiliary air force of the British Royal Air Force.
Major League Baseball pitcher Don Larsen threw the only perfect game in World Series history.
Marxist revolutionary and guerrilla leader Che Guevara was captured near La Higuera, Bolivia.
A new airport for Oslo, Norway, opened at Gardermoen, replacing a smaller one at the same location that had served as a backup to the city's previous main airport at Fornebu.
At Linate Airport in Milan, Italy, Scandinavian Airlines Flight SK686 collided on take-off with a Cessna Citation II business jet, killing 118 people.
Yemen War: A funeral in Sanaa was hit by two consecutive airstrikes by a Saudi -led coalition, leaving 143–155 civilians dead and more than 525 injured.

links.title: Saudi-led intervention in the Yemeni civil war

facts.text: In the American Civil War, the Battle of Perryville was fought west of Perryville, Kentucky.
Three trains collided at Harrow & Wealdstone station in London, killing 112 people and injuring 340 others.
Demonstrations organized by the Weather Underground known as the Days of Rage began in Chicago, aimed at ending U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War.

links.title: Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War

facts.text: The Croatian Army and Croatian Defence Council launched Operation Southern Move, their last offensive in the Bosnian War.
Anti-government protests calling for free and fair elections began in Baku, Azerbaijan.
Late in the Napoleonic Wars, Empress Marie Louise issued decrees conscripting tens of thousands of French teenagers, who became known as Marie-Louises.

The Universal Postal Union, then known as the General Postal Union, was established with the signing of the Treaty of Bern to unify disparate postal services and regulations so that international mail could be exchanged easily.
World War I: The civilian authorities of Antwerp surrendered and allowed the German army to capture the city.
Syrian civil war: Turkish forces began an offensive into north-eastern Syria following the withdrawal of U.S. troops from the region.

links.title: Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria

facts.text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek wrote a letter to the Royal Society describing " animalcules " – the first known description of protozoa.
The deadliest Atlantic hurricane on record began to impact the Caribbean, killing at least 20,000 people across the Antilles over the subsequent days.
The Washington Monument in Washington, D.C., at the time the world's tallest building, officially opened to the general public.

links.title: List of tallest buildings and structures

facts.text: Carrying a cargo hold full of highly flammable chemicals, the ocean liner SS Volturno caught fire in the north Atlantic and sank, resulting in 136 deaths.
World War II: American forces defeated the Japanese at the Third Battle of the Matanikau in Guadalcanal, Solomon Islands, reversing the Japanese victory a couple of weeks earlier.
Nick Holonyak, an engineer for General Electric, gave the first public demonstration of a light-emitting diode.
The Phantom of the Opera, a musical by Andrew Lloyd Webber and currently the longest-running Broadway show in history, opened in London's West End.

links.title: The Phantom of the Opera (1986 musical)
List of the longest-running Broadway shows

facts.text: Pakistani activist Malala Yousafzai was severely injured by a Taliban gunman in a failed assassination attempt.
Great Northern War: Russia defeated Sweden at the Battle of Lesnaya on the Russian–Polish border, in present-day Belarus.
European soldiers and Javanese collaborators started massacring Chinese Indonesians (depicted) in the port city of Batavia, modern-day Jakarta: at least 10,000 people were killed.
French Revolution: After a month-long siege, the leaders of Lyon surrendered, ending their revolt against the National Convention.

links.title: Revolt of Lyon against the National Convention

facts.text: Following a reduction in pay, textile workers in Little Falls, New York, walked out of their mill, starting a three-month strike.
A footman shot and killed two colleagues and wounded the lady of the house at Knowsley Hall, England.
English astronomer William Lassell discovered Triton, the largest moon of Neptune.
Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union, a militant organisation campaigning for women's suffrage in the United Kingdom.

links.title: Women's suffrage in the United Kingdom

facts.text: In the first proven act of sabotage in the history of commercial aviation, a Boeing 247 operated by United Airlines exploded in mid-air near Chesterton, Indiana, killing all seven people aboard.
The Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, which prohibits all test detonations of nuclear weapons except for those conducted underground, went into effect.
U.S. vice president Spiro Agnew resigned after being charged with tax evasion.
After 20 years of construction, Vidyasagar Setu, the longest cable-stayed bridge in India, opened, joining Kolkata and Howrah.
Husayn ibn Ali, a grandson of Muhammad, was killed at the Battle of Karbala (depicted) by the forces of Yazid I, whom Husayn had refused to recognize as caliph.
In a treaty with Dutch colonial authorities, the Ndyuka people of Suriname gained territorial autonomy.
The Xinhai Revolution began with the Wuchang Uprising, marking the beginning of the collapse of the Qing dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China.

World War II: The Kempeitai, the military police arm of the Imperial Japanese Army, arrested and tortured fifty-seven civilians and civilian internees on suspicion of their involvement in a raid on Singapore Harbour.
Eight-year-old Huang Na was abducted and murdered; her body was found three weeks later after a search across Singapore and Malaysia.
French Revolutionary Wars: The Royal Navy captured eleven Dutch Navy ships without any losses at the Battle of Camperdown.
Bashir Shihab II surrendered to the Ottoman Empire and was removed as Emir of Mount Lebanon after an imperial decree by Sultan Abdülmecid I.
World War II: At the Battle of Cape Esperance on the northwest coast of Guadalcanal, American ships intercepted and defeated a Japanese fleet sent to attack Henderson Field.

A field-sequential color system developed by Hungarian-American engineer Peter Goldmark became the first color television system to be adopted for commercial use, only for it to be abandoned a year later.
Typhoon Nora, the fourth-most intense tropical cyclone on record, dissipated after killing 40 people and leaving more than a million homeless across Taiwan and the Philippines.
The Treaty of Shaoxing was ratified, ending the Jin–Song wars, although sporadic fighting continued until 1234.
The University of Sydney, Australia's oldest university, was inaugurated two years after being established by the University of Sydney Act.
The Morant Bay rebellion, led by Paul Bogle and George William Gordon, began in Jamaica; after protestors burned down the courthouse, it was brutally suppressed by Governor Edward John Eyre.

Former British king Edward and his wife arrived at Berlin Friedrichstraße station to begin a tour of Nazi Germany, where they were greeted with Nazi salutes and dined with high-ranking members of the state apparatus.

links.title: 1937 tour of Germany by the Duke and Duchess of Windsor

facts.text: CBS 's field-sequential color system for television was the first to be licensed for broadcast by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission.
Apollo 7, the first manned mission of NASA 's Apollo program, and the first three-man American space mission, launched from Complex 34 in Cape Kennedy, Florida.
Sri Lankan Civil War: The Indian Peace Keeping Force began Operation Pawan to take control of Jaffna from the Tamil Tigers and enforce their disarmament as a part of the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord.
A bomb exploded in the Myyrmanni shopping center in Helsinki, Finland, resulting in seven deaths and 159 injuries.
The peerage and clergy of the Kingdom of England published the Ordinances of 1311 to restrict King Edward II 's powers.

American Revolutionary War: A British fleet defeated American ships at the Battle of Valcour Island on Lake Champlain, but gave American forces enough time to prepare their defenses for the Saratoga campaign.
In Washington, D.C., the Daughters of the American Revolution was founded.
Aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger, astronaut Kathryn D. Sullivan became the first American woman to perform a space walk.

image.caption: Born Kathryn Dwyer Sullivan ( 1951-10-03 ) October 3, 1951 (age 74) Paterson, New Jersey , U.S.

facts.text: An estimated 750,000 people attended the " Great March " in Washington, D.C., to demand greater civil rights for the LGBT community.

links.title: Second National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights

facts.text: Believing he had reached the East Indies, Christopher Columbus made landfall on an island in the Caribbean, sparking a series of events that led to the European colonization of the Americas.
Jeanne Geneviève Garnerin became the first woman to make a parachute descent, falling 900 metres (3,000 ft) in the gondola of a hot air balloon.
The Uddevalla Suffrage Association was founded in Uddevalla, Sweden, with the purpose of bringing about universal suffrage.
The Pledge of Allegiance of the United States was first used in public schools to coincide with the opening of the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
The iron lung, a type of medical ventilator, was used for the first time at the Boston Children's Hospital to treat an eight-year-old girl paralyzed by polio.
The United States Department of Justice acquired a military prison on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay, to be transformed into the last-resort Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary.
Il Canto degli Italiani is adopted as national anthem by the newly formed Italian Republic.
Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev reportedly pounded his shoe on a desk during a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly in protest at a speech by Philippine delegate Lorenzo Sumulong.
While in prison for murder, boxer James Scott defeated Eddie "The Flame" Gregory, a leading light heavyweight.
The Provisional Irish Republican Army detonated a bomb at the Grand Hotel in Brighton, England, in a failed attempt to assassinate British prime minister Margaret Thatcher and her cabinet.
An earthquake with a magnitude of 5.8 or 5.9 struck south of Cairo, Egypt, killing 545 people.
Twelve people were killed in an apartment-building collapse in Medellín, leading to new construction laws being passed in Colombia.
Chen Yanxiang, the only person from Indonesia known to have visited dynastic Korea, reached Seoul after having set out from Java four months before.
The Peasants' War began in Overmere, Southern Netherlands, with peasants taking up arms against the French occupiers.
First World War: New Zealand troops suffered more than 2,000 casualties, including more than 800 deaths, in the First Battle of Passchendaele, making it the nation's largest loss of life in one day.
Japan Socialist Party leader Inejirō Asanuma was assassinated during a live television recording by a far-right ultra-nationalist using a short sword.
Typhoon Tip, the largest and most intense tropical cyclone ever recorded, reached a worldwide record-low sea-level pressure of 870 mbar (25.69 inHg ) in the western Pacific Ocean.
Goguryeo–Tang War: Led by Emperor Taizong, the Tang army was forced to abandon a siege of Ansi Fortress.

links.title: First conflict of the Goguryeo–Tang War

facts.text: Agents of King Philip IV of France launched a raid on the Knights Templar at dawn, arresting many members, subsequently torturing them into giving false confessions and burning them at the stake.
French astronomer Charles Messier discovered the Whirlpool Galaxy, an interacting, grand design spiral galaxy located an estimated 31 million light-years away.
War of 1812: After three days of fighting, the beached U.S. Revenue Cutter Service vessel Eagle was captured by the Royal Navy.
Prince Arthur, a son of Queen Victoria, became the first Governor General of Canada of royal descent, as well as the first Prince of Great Britain and Ireland to hold that position.

links.title: Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught and Strathearn

facts.text: At least 30,000 people witnessed the Miracle of the Sun in the fields of Cova da Iria near Fátima, Portugal.

The Soviet republics of Russia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia signed the Treaty of Kars with the Grand National Assembly of Turkey, establishing the current borders between Turkey and the Caucasian states.
Newly elected Burundian prime minister Louis Rwagasore was assassinated by his political rivals.
Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 crashed into a remote area in the Andes mountains near the border of Chile and Argentina; the 16 remaining survivors were not rescued until more than two months later.
The Dragon King of Bhutan, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck married Jetsun Pema at the Punakha Dzong.
During the Hindu festival of Navaratri at a temple in Madhya Pradesh, India, rumours about an impending bridge collapse caused a stampede that resulted in 115 deaths.
The King of Thailand, Bhumibol Adulyadej, died after 70 years on the throne, at which point was the longest-reigning current monarch.

links.title: Death and funeral of Bhumibol Adulyadej

facts.text: Queen Anne's War: French and Wabanaki forces surrendered to end the Siege of Port Royal, giving the British permanent possession of Nova Scotia.
War of 1812: British troops and Mohawk warriors repelled an American invasion from across the Niagara River at the Battle of Queenston Heights near Queenston, Ontario.
British suffragette Margaret Travers Symons became the first woman to speak in the House of Commons when she escaped from her escort into the chamber and shouted at the assembly.

links.title: House of Commons of the United Kingdom

facts.text: The Troubles: In a meeting at Fernhill House, Belfast, loyalist leader Gusty Spence announced that the Combined Loyalist Military Command would observe a ceasefire.
At the Chicago Marathon, Kenyan runner Brigid Kosgei set the current marathon world record for women running in a mixed-sex race.
Forces of the Burmese Toungoo dynasty led by King Tabinshwehti (depicted) departed Martaban to begin an invasion of the Ayutthaya Kingdom.

Third Silesian War: At the Battle of Hochkirch, an Austrian army under Leopold Joseph von Daun surprised the Prussians commanded by Frederick the Great, overwhelming them and forcing a general retreat.
American Civil War: In the Battle of Bristoe Station, the Union II Corps surprised and repelled the Confederate attack on the Union rearguard, resulting in a Union victory.
French inventor Louis Le Prince filmed Roundhay Garden Scene, the earliest surviving motion picture, in Leeds, England.
The first book featuring English author A. A. Milne 's fictional bear Winnie-the-Pooh was published.
Second World War: The German submarine U-47 torpedoed and sank the Royal Navy battleship HMS Royal Oak while the latter was anchored at Scapa Flow in Orkney, Scotland.
Second World War: During the Blitz, a semi-armour-piercing fragmentation bomb fell on the road above Balham station in London, which was being used as an air raid shelter, killing at least 64 people.
World War II: During the second raid on Schweinfurt, the U.S. 8th Air Force suffered so many losses that it lost air supremacy over Germany for several months.
The Holocaust: Prisoners at Sobibor extermination camp revolted, killing 11 SS officers and staging a mass escape.
American test pilot Chuck Yeager became the first person to break the sound barrier, reaching Mach 1.06 on board the Bell X-1, an experimental rocket-powered aircraft.
The first of the Smith Act trials concluded in New York City, with eleven leaders of the Communist Party of the United States found guilty of violating the Smith Act.

links.title: Smith Act trials of Communist Party leaders
Communist Party of the United States

facts.text: Israeli military commander Ariel Sharon and his Unit 101 special forces attacked the village of Qibya on the West Bank, destroying 45 buildings, killing 42 villagers, and wounding 15 others.
The Queen Elizabeth Way, North America's first intercity divided highway, opens.
B. R. Ambedkar, a leader of India's " Untouchable " caste, publicly converted to Buddhism and became the leader of the Dalit Buddhist movement.
After three days of heavy rain, the Turia overflowed and flooded the city of Valencia, Spain, causing at least 81 deaths.
At least 75,000 people attended the National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights in Washington, D.C., to demand equal civil rights for LGBT people.

links.title: National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights

facts.text: The 6th Congress of the Workers' Party concluded, having anointed North Korean president Kim Il Sung 's son Kim Jong Il as his successor.

links.title: 6th Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea

facts.text: Michael Woodford was dismissed as the CEO of the optics manufacturer Olympus after uncovering internal financial misconduct, escalating the corporate scandal into one of the largest in Japanese business history.
Felix Baumgartner jumped from a helium balloon in the stratosphere to become the first person to break the sound barrier without vehicular power.
A snowstorm and series of avalanches occurred on and around the Himalayan peaks of Annapurna and Dhaulagiri, resulting in the deaths of at least 43 people.
Approximately 10,000 John Deere employees went on strike in one of the largest private-sector strikes in the United States.
Norman Conquest: William the Conqueror 's forces defeated the English army at Hastings and killed Harold Godwinson (depicted), the last crowned Anglo-Saxon king of England.
War of the Third Coalition: French forces under Marshal Michel Ney defeated Austrian forces in Elchingen, present-day Germany.
The worst mining accident in the United Kingdom's history took place when an explosion resulted in 440 deaths at the Universal Colliery in Senghenydd, Wales.
The Second Philippine Republic, a Japanese puppet state, was established with Jose P. Laurel as its first president.
Members of the Politburo voted to remove Nikita Khrushchev as First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and replace him with Leonid Brezhnev.

links.title: Politburo of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union
General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union

facts.text: American Civil War: Confederate forces captured Glasgow, Missouri, although it had little long-term benefit as Price's Missouri Expedition was defeated a week later.

The Motherland Calls (depicted in coat of arms), a colossal statue in Volgograd, Russia, which commemorates the casualties of the Battle of Stalingrad, was dedicated, becoming the then-tallest statue in the world.

New Zealand Police conducted several anti-terrorism raids in relation to the discovery of an alleged paramilitary training camp in the Urewera mountain ranges, arresting 17 people and seizing four guns and 230 rounds of ammunition.
Global demonstrations against economic inequality, corporate influence on government, and other issues, were held in more than 950 cities in 82 countries.
Ottoman–Habsburg wars: The siege of Vienna ended with Austrian forces repelling the invading Turks, turning the tide against almost a century of conquest in Europe by the Ottoman Empire.
The "From Hell" letter, allegedly from Jack the Ripper, was sent to George Lusk, the chairman of the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee in London.
Vietnam War protests: At an anti-war rally in New York City, David J. Miller burned his draft card, the first such act to result in arrest under a new amendment to the Selective Service Act.

links.title: Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War

facts.text: President Carlos Humberto Romero of El Salvador was overthrown and exiled in a military coup d'état.
A 7.2-magnitude earthquake struck Bohol in the Philippines, resulting in 222 deaths.
Thirteen-year-old Jayme Closs was kidnapped from her home in Barron, Wisconsin, and held captive for 88 days.
Napoleon began his exile on Saint Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean, which would encompass his final six years.
Air India, the flag carrier airline of India, began operations under the name Tata Airlines.
Hurricane Hazel made landfall in the Carolinas in the United States before moving north to Toronto in Canada later the same day, killing 176 people in the two countries.
The Irish Criminal Assets Bureau was established following the gangland murders of Detective Garda Jerry McCabe and investigative journalist Veronica Guerin.
An earthquake registering 6.7 M w occurred off the northwestern coast of the island of Hawaii.
War of the First Coalition: The two-day Battle of Wattignies concluded with Jean-Baptiste Jourdan leading French forces to victory over Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld.
The Sixth Coalition attacked French forces led by Napoleon in the Battle of Leipzig, the largest conflict in the Napoleonic Wars, with over 500,000 troops involved.
Most of the Palace of Westminster in London was destroyed in a fire caused by the burning of wooden tally sticks.
The Church of Scotland established Queen's College in Kingston, Ontario, in Canada.
Margaret Sanger established the United States' first family planning clinic in Brooklyn, New York.

image.caption: Born Margaret Louise Higgins ( 1879-09-14 ) September 14, 1879 Corning, New York , U.S.

facts.text: Roy and Walt Disney founded the Disney Brothers Cartoon Studio in Hollywood, which eventually grew to become one of the largest media and entertainment corporations in the world.

image.caption: The Walt Disney Studios , the company's headquarters in Burbank, California, in 2016

facts.text: The Holocaust: The Gestapo conducted a raid on the Roman Ghetto, capturing 1,259 members of the Jewish community, most of whom were sent to Auschwitz.

links.title: History of the Jews in Italy

facts.text: A four-day air battle over Taiwan ended with a decisive American victory, destroying hundreds of Japanese aircraft and military facilities.
With the success of Project 596, China became the world's fifth nuclear power.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize would be jointly awarded to Henry Kissinger and Lê Đức Thọ, sparking international controversy.
A man drove his vehicle through the window of a Luby's Cafeteria in Killeen, Texas, and opened fire, killing 23 people before fatally shooting himself.
In Laos's deadliest air accident, Lao Airlines Flight 301 crashed into the Mekong River, resulting in the deaths of all 49 people aboard.
Jadwiga was officially crowned as " King of Poland " instead of "Queen" to reflect the fact that she was a sovereign in her own right.
Brigham Young University was founded in Provo, Utah, United States.
Authorities of the British Raj partitioned the Bengal Presidency, separating the largely Muslim eastern areas from the largely Hindu western areas.
The first novel of the The Chronicles of Narnia series by C. S. Lewis, The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, was published in the United Kingdom.

links.title: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

facts.text: The Maltese journalist and anti-corruption activist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bomb attack in Bidnija.
German astronomer Johannes Kepler began observations of an exceptionally bright object, now known as Kepler's Supernova, that had appeared in the constellation Ophiuchus.
American Revolutionary War: British general John Burgoyne 's Saratoga campaign ended with his surrender to the Americans, later convincing France to enter the war in alliance with the United States.

links.title: France in the American Revolutionary War

facts.text: A wooden beer-fermenting vat in London burst, destroying a second vat and causing a large flood of at least 128,000 imperial gallons (580,000 l; 154,000 US gal) of porter that killed eight people.
Off the coast of the Dutch island of Texel, a British naval squadron sank the German 7th Half Flotilla of torpedo boats in the Battle off Texel.
Prime Minister Robert Menzies inaugurated the artificial Lake Burley Griffin in the centre of the Australian capital Canberra.

image.caption: Lake Burley Griffin Show map of Australian Capital Territory Lake Burley Griffin Show map of Australia

facts.text: Hundred Years' War: Under the terms of Scotland's Auld Alliance with France, King David II of Scotland was captured at the Battle of Neville's Cross following his invasion of England.

image.caption: Date 17 October 1346 Location Neville's Cross , west of Durham , England 54°46′21″N 01°35′36″W ﻿ / ﻿ 54.77250°N 1.59333°W ﻿ / 54.77250; -1.59333 Result English victory Capture of the Scottish King

facts.text: American gangster Al Capone was convicted on five counts of income-tax evasion.
Indonesian Army elements surrounded the Merdeka Palace in Jakarta, demanding that President Sukarno disband the Provisional People's Representative Council.
Yom Kippur War: Egyptian forces retreated from the Battle of the Chinese Farm, allowing Israeli forces to build their first bridge across the Suez Canal.

A fatal rail crash at Hatfield, Hertfordshire, led to the introduction of widespread speed limit reductions throughout the British rail network and eventually caused the collapse of the railway management group Railtrack.
A series of executions of the commissioners who signed the death warrant of King Charles I of England concluded; six were hanged, drawn and quartered for treason.

links.title: List of regicides of Charles I

facts.text: Ascanio in Alba, an opera composed by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart at the age of 15, premiered in Milan.
The Open Championship, the oldest of the four major championships in men's golf, was first played at Prestwick Golf Club in Scotland.
Having gone to the wrong house in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, for a Halloween party, Japanese exchange student Yoshihiro Hattori was shot and killed by the homeowner.
Rehavam Ze'evi, the Israeli minister of tourism, was assassinated in revenge for the killing of PFLP leader Abu Ali Mustafa.

links.title: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine

facts.text: Pappus of Alexandria, one of the last great Greek mathematicians of antiquity, observed an eclipse that allowed historians to calculate the approximate dates of his life.
Byzantine–Norman wars: Robert Guiscard led an invasion of the Byzantine Empire, capturing Dyrrhachium in present-day Albania.
The first recorded naval battle between Europeans and the Japanese occurred when a flotilla of samurai attacked two Portuguese trade vessels at the Battle of Fukuda Bay in Nagasaki.
Filipino sailors disembarked from the Manila galleon Nuestra Señora de Buena Esperanza in what is now Morro Bay, California, the first documented instance of Asians in the Americas.

links.title: First landing of Filipinos in the United States

facts.text: The War of the Austrian Succession ended with the signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.
Renton defeated Kilmarnock 2–0 in the opening match of the inaugural Scottish Cup.
The Robert Burns Memorial Statue, the first public statue erected in New Brunswick, was dedicated in Fredericton.
The Soviet space probe Venera 4 became the first spacecraft to perform direct in situ analysis of the environment of another planet ( Venus ).
At the Summer Olympics in Mexico City, American athlete Bob Beamon achieved a distance of 8.90 m (29.2 ft) in the long jump event, setting a world record that stood for 23 years.

links.title: Athletics at the 1968 Summer Olympics – Men's long jump
Men's long jump world record progression

facts.text: Nihilism, the first professional runway show from the British designer Alexander McQueen, was staged in London.
The most significant earthquake to have occurred in Central Europe in recorded history destroyed Basel, Switzerland.
American Revolutionary War: In an act of retaliation against ports that supported Patriot activities in the early stages of the war, the Royal Navy destroyed what is now Portland, Maine.
Johannes Brahms conducted the premiere of his Double Concerto, composed for violinist Joseph Joachim and cellist Robert Hausmann.
The first cat in space, later known as Félicette, launched aboard a French Véronique rocket.
Protests in Santiago that started 11 days prior escalated into open battle against the Chilean national police, forcing President Sebastián Piñera to declare a state of emergency.
A ceremony was held in Edinburgh marking the coming of age of James VI of Scotland as an adult ruler.

links.title: Entry of James VI into Edinburgh

facts.text: The Pennsylvania Gazette published a statement by Benjamin Franklin describing a kite experiment (depicted) to determine the electrical nature of lightning.
First World War: Allied forces began engaging German troops at the First Battle of Ypres.
The Guatemalan Revolution began with a small group of army officers led by Francisco Javier Arana and Jacobo Árbenz launching a coup against dictator Jorge Ubico.
The Spanish ship San Felipe was shipwrecked on the Japanese island of Shikoku, and its cargo confiscated by the local daimyo.
American Revolutionary War: British forces led by Lord Cornwallis officially surrendered to Franco-American forces under George Washington and the comte de Rochambeau, ending the Siege of Yorktown.

links.title: Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, comte de Rochambeau

facts.text: A group of ethnic Hutu military officers failed in their attempt to overthrow the Burundian government.
Iran–Iraq War: U.S. Navy forces destroyed two Iranian oil platforms in the Persian Gulf in response to an Iranian missile attack on a Kuwaiti oil tanker three days earlier.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 22.6 percent on Black Monday, the largest one-day percentage decline in the stock market index's history.

links.title: List of largest daily changes in the Dow Jones Industrial Average

facts.text: The British government restricted the broadcast of the voices of representatives from Sinn Féin and several Irish republican and loyalist paramilitary groups on television and radio.
British YouTube collective the Sidemen were formed as a Rockstar Games Social Club group in Grand Theft Auto Online.
Canadian astronomer Robert Weryk discovered ʻOumuamua (depicted), the first known interstellar object detected passing through the Solar System.
American Civil War: Despite incurring nearly twice as many casualties as the Confederates, the Union army emerged victorious at the Battle of Cedar Creek.
World War II: Allied aircraft sank the German cargo ship Sinfra, killing mostly Italian POWs.
At a meeting of its general assembly, the European Broadcasting Union approved the staging of the first Eurovision Song Contest.

links.title: History of the Eurovision Song Contest

facts.text: Vietnam War: The Siege of Plei Me began with the first major confrontation between soldiers of the North Vietnamese Army and the U.S. Army.
Hurricane Wilma became the most intense Atlantic hurricane on record with a minimum atmospheric pressure of 882 mbar (26.05 inHg ).
Under the terms of the Pragmatic Sanction, Maria Theresa ascended the Habsburg throne.
Pope Pius XII published his first encyclical, Summi Pontificatus, which critiqued ideologies such as racism, cultural superiority and totalitarianism.

African-American college football player Johnny Bright was the victim of an on-field assault, eventually leading to changes in NCAA football rules that mandated the use of more protective helmets with face guards.
Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin filmed an unidentified subject, which they claimed was Bigfoot, at Six Rivers National Forest in California.
Experimental results from the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center were published showing that protons were composed of smaller particles, the first evidence of quarks.
Three members of the American rock band Lynyrd Skynyrd died when their chartered plane crashed in Gillsburg, Mississippi.
During a UEFA Cup match between Spartak Moscow and Haarlem, a large number of attendees trying to leave the Central Lenin Stadium resulted in a stampede that caused 66 deaths.
The Spanish trawler Sonia sank in British waters after a five-hour chase by the Irish Naval Service patrol vessel Aisling, during which almost 600 shots were fired.

links.title: Sinking of the Spanish trawler Sonia

facts.text: Aeroflot Flight 6502 crashed on approach to Kurumoch Airport in Samara, Russia (then Kuybyshev in the Soviet Union), killing 70 people on board.
An earthquake struck the Indian state of Uttarakhand, killing at least 768 people and destroying thousands of homes.
First Libyan Civil War: Muammar Gaddafi, the deposed Libyan leader, was captured by rebel forces during the Battle of Sirte, and was killed shortly thereafter.
British woman Mabel Freer was refused entry to Australia after failing a dictation test given in Italian, leading to a debate over Australia's immigration policy.
World War II: Fulfilling a promise he made two years previously, General Douglas MacArthur landed on Leyte to begin the recapture of the Philippines.

links.title: Douglas MacArthur's escape from the Philippines

facts.text: Watergate scandal: Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy William Ruckelshaus resigned after refusing to obey President Richard Nixon 's order to have Archibald Cox fired.
Protests broke out across Chad after President Mahamat Déby declared his intentions to extend his rule by another two years.
Prabowo Subianto and Gibran Rakabuming Raka were sworn in as president and vice president of Indonesia, becoming the oldest and the youngest person to assume respective offices.
Hundred Years' War: The English victory at the Battle of Auberoche marked a change in the military balance of power in Aquitaine, with the subsequent collapse of the French position.

French composer Jacques Offenbach 's operetta Orpheus in the Underworld, featuring the music most associated with the can-can (audio featured), was first performed at the Théâtre des Bouffes-Parisiens in Paris.

The first and second of three treaties were signed near Medicine Lodge, Kansas, between the United States federal government and several Native American tribes in the Great Plains, requiring them to relocate to areas in present-day western Oklahoma.
HMS Niobe arrived in Halifax Harbour to become the first large ship of the Royal Canadian Navy.
World War II: German soldiers massacred nearly 2,800 Serbs in Kragujevac in reprisal for insurgent attacks in the district of Gornji Milanovac.
The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright, opened in New York City.
At the height of the Japanese university protests, protesters occupied Shinjuku Station in Tokyo and clashed violently with police.
North Korea and the United States signed the Agreed Framework to limit the former's nuclear weapons program and to normalize relations between the two countries.

links.title: North Korea and weapons of mass destruction

facts.text: First Crusade: At the Battle of Civetot, the Seljuk forces of Kilij Arslan destroyed the army of the People's Crusade as it marched toward Nicaea.
Florence Nightingale and a staff of 38 nurses and 15 nuns were sent to the Ottoman Empire to help treat wounded British soldiers fighting in the Crimean War.
World War II: The three-week-long Battle of Aachen concluded, making the city the first on German soil to be captured by the Allies.
A coal tip fell on the village of Aberfan, Wales, killing 144 people, mostly schoolchildren.
In Seoul, South Korea, 32 people were killed and 17 others injured when a span of the Seongsu Bridge collapsed.
Ahmad ibn Kayghalagh, an Abbasid military officer of Turkic origin, led a raid against the Byzantine Empire, taking at least 4,000 captives.

At the Battle of Liaoluo Bay Ming Chinese naval forces defeated a Dutch East India Company fleet in the Taiwan Strait, the largest naval encounter between Chinese and European forces before the First Opium War more than two hundred years later.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of the chorale cantata Schmücke dich, o liebe Seele (Adorn yourself, O dear soul), based on the communion hymn of the same name, in Leipzig.

links.title: Schmücke dich, o liebe Seele, BWV 180

facts.text: George II and Caroline of Ansbach were crowned king and queen of Great Britain in Westminster Abbey.

image.caption: King of Great Britain and Ireland Elector of Hanover

links.title: Coronation of George II and Caroline

facts.text: A two-week massacre of ethnic Chinese in Batavia, Dutch East Indies, came to an end with at least 10,000 people killed.
Scotland's worst mining accident occurred when an explosion at a colliery in Blantyre, South Lanarkshire, killed 207 miners.
At Gare Montparnasse in Paris, an express train derailed after overrunning the buffer stop and crashed through the station wall, with the locomotive landing on the street below.
A bank run forced New York's Knickerbocker Trust Company to suspend operations, triggering the Panic of 1907.
The educational non-profit organization Toastmasters International was founded at a YMCA in Santa Ana, California.
The Royal Navy cutlass was withdrawn from combat service.
Dod Orsborne, captain of the Girl Pat, was convicted of its theft and imprisoned, having caused a media sensation when it went missing.
With their album The Supremes A' Go-Go, the Supremes became the first all-female group to reach number one on the Billboard 200 chart.
John Adams' opera Nixon in China premiered.
In Ottawa, Canada, the downtown core was placed on lockdown after a series of shootings at Parliament Hill.
A sword-wielding man attacked students and teachers at a high school in Trollhättan, killing three people in Sweden's deadliest school attack.
In one of the worst maritime disasters in the history of the British Isles, at least 1,400 sailors on four Royal Navy ships were lost in stormy weather off the Isles of Scilly.
After evading Vichy French and Francoist Spanish authorities, Belgian prime minister Hubert Pierlot arrived in London, marking the beginning of the Belgian government in exile.
Workers at the Cigar Factory in Charleston, South Carolina, began a labor strike against the American Tobacco Company that lasted more than five months.
The first volume of Ian Fleming 's children's novel Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang was published posthumously.
TAN-SAHSA Flight 414 crashed in approach to Toncontín International Airport killing 131 out of 146 people onboard.
Bellview Airlines Flight 210 crashed in Ogun State, Nigeria, killing all 117 people on board.
Irish Catholic gentry in Ulster tried to seize control of Dublin Castle, the seat of English rule in Ireland, to force concessions to Catholics.
Jeannette Piccard piloted a hot-air balloon flight that reached 57,579 feet (17,550 m), becoming the first woman to fly in the stratosphere.

image.caption: Born Jeannette Ridlon ( 1895-01-05 ) January 5, 1895 Chicago, Illinois, U.S.

facts.text: A screening of Mother India, one of the most influential Indian films in history, was held for President Rajendra Prasad and Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru two days before its release.
The runway show for Alexander McQueen 's collection The Hunger was staged at London's Natural History Museum.
An escalator accident in Rome left 24 people injured, mostly fans of the CSKA Moscow football team who were in town for a UEFA Champions League match against Roma.
War of the Second Coalition: The Ottoman–Albanian forces of Ali Pasha of Janina defeated French troops and captured the town of Preveza at the Battle of Nicopolis.
The inaugural National Women's Rights Convention, presided over by American activist Paulina Wright Davis, began in Worcester, Massachusetts.
The State of Vietnam voted in a referendum to become a republic.
Vietnam War: Operation Linebacker, a U.S. bombing campaign against North Vietnam in response to its Easter Offensive, ended after five months.
Grand Theft Auto III was released, helping to popularize open-world and mature-content video games.
Hurricane Patricia, the most intense tropical cyclone on record in the Western Hemisphere, peaked with maximum sustained winds of 215 mph (345 km/h) south of Mexico.
Myanmar civil war: Burmese military forces launched airstrikes that killed at least 80 concertgoers in Kachin State.
The Battle of Grathe Heath ended the Danish Civil War.
Alberto Santos-Dumont flew his biplane 14-bis for 50 metres (160 ft) at an altitude of about four metres (13 ft).
World War II: Japanese troops began an unsuccessful attempt to recapture Henderson Field on Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands from American forces.
The Hungarian Revolution began as a peaceful student demonstration that attracted thousands while marching through central Budapest to the parliament building.
During the Malaysian motorcycle Grand Prix, Marco Simoncelli collided with two other riders, resulting in his death due to serious trauma to the head, neck, and chest.
Qutuz, the sultan of Egypt, was assassinated and replaced by fellow Mamluk leader Baybars.
War of the First Coalition: The Battle of Schliengen was fought between the French and Austrian armies, who both claimed victory.
The Brabant Revolution, sometimes considered to be the first expression of Belgian nationalism, began with the invasion of the Austrian Netherlands by an émigré army from the Dutch Republic.
William Lassell found Umbriel and Ariel, the third and fourth Uranian moons to be discovered.
Sir Henry Parkes, Premier of the Colony of New South Wales, gave a speech in which he called for the federation of the six Australian colonies.
The George Washington Bridge, connecting New York City to Fort Lee, New Jersey, and today the world's busiest motor-vehicle bridge, was dedicated.
World War II: The Japanese battleship Musashi, one of the heaviest and most powerfully armed ever constructed, was sunk by American aircraft during the Battle of Leyte Gulf.
The Charter of the United Nations entered into force after being ratified by the five permanent members of the Security Council and a majority of the other signatories.

links.title: Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council

facts.text: The cornerstone of the United Nations headquarters was laid in New York City.
Charges in a military court against generals Dương Văn Đức and Lâm Văn Phát of leading a coup attempt against South Vietnamese leader Nguyễn Khánh, were dropped..
Three people were killed when falsework collapsed during the construction of the Loddon Bridge in Berkshire, leading to reform of construction practices in the UK.
In protest against wage discrepancy and unfair employment practices, 90 percent of Iceland's female population went on strike for a day.
The inaugural Afro-Asian Games opened in Hyderabad, with 2,040 athletes from 96 nations competing.
The Russian ship Dmitry ran aground in Whitby, an incident that inspired the arrival of Count Dracula to England in Bram Stoker 's 1897 novel.
On " Black Thursday ", the New York Stock Exchange lost 11 percent of its value at the opening bell on very heavy trading, marking the beginning of the Great Depression.
The Pacification Junta deposed Brazillian president Washington Luís, ending the Brazilian Revolution of 1930.
English football club Manchester United defeated rivals Arsenal 2–0 in the Battle of the Buffet, ending the latter's record-breaking unbeaten run.

links.title: List of unbeaten football club seasons

facts.text: Lam Wing-kee, the owner of Causeway Bay Books in Hong Kong, known for publishing political books banned in mainland China, was abducted by Chinese authorities.
Hundred Years' War: The army of Henry V of England, consisting mostly of archers, unexpectedly defeated the numerically superior French cavalry at the Battle of Agincourt on Saint Crispin's Day.

image.caption: Date 25 October 1415 ( Saint Crispin's Day ) Location Azincourt , County of Saint-Pol (now Pas-de-Calais ) 50°27′49″N 2°8′30″E ﻿ / ﻿ 50.46361°N 2.14167°E ﻿ / 50.46361; 2.14167 Result English victory

facts.text: Dutch explorer Dirk Hartog left a plate on an island in Shark Bay, the oldest-known artefact of European exploration in Australia still in existence.
George III became King of Great Britain and Ireland, succeeding his grandfather George II.
Crimean War: The ill-fated Charge of the Light Brigade was decisively repelled by Russian forces during the Battle of Balaclava.
American Civil War: During Price's Missouri Expedition, Union troops defeated Sterling Price 's Confederate army in three successive battles: Marais des Cygnes, Mine Creek, and Marmiton River.
The Italian cruise liner SS Principessa Mafalda sank when a propeller shaft broke and fractured the hull, resulting in 314 deaths.
Heinrich Himmler ordered a crackdown on the Edelweiss Pirates, a nonconformist youth group that assisted army deserters and others hiding from the Nazis.

The People's Volunteer Army ambushed the South Korean II Corps at the Battle of Onjong, and elsewhere engaged the 1st Infantry Division at the Battle of Unsan, marking China's entry into the Korean War.
Windows XP, one of the most popular and widely used versions of the Microsoft Windows operating system, was released for retail sale.
At 49 days, Liz Truss concluded the shortest tenure as prime minister of the United Kingdom.

links.title: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

facts.text: Reconquista: Forces under Afonso I of Portugal captured Lisbon from the Moors after a four-month siege (depicted) in one of the few Christian victories during the Second Crusade.
Irish playwright and politician Terence MacSwiney died after a hunger strike in Brixton Prison, bringing the Irish struggle for independence to international attention.
The Daily Mail published the Zinoviev letter, a hoax purported to be a directive from Moscow to increase communist agitation.
USS Tang, the U.S. Navy submarine credited with sinking more ships than any other American submarine, sank when it was struck by its own torpedo.
Mount Merapi in Central Java, Indonesia, began an increasingly violent series of eruptions that lasted over a month.
The Byzantine army proclaimed chief minister John VI Kantakouzenos as emperor, triggering a civil war between his supporters and those of John V Palaiologos, the heir to the throne.
Imjin War: Thirteen Korean ships commanded by Admiral Yi Sun-sin defeated a far larger Japanese invading fleet at the Battle of Myeongnyang in the Myeongnyang Strait.
War of 1812: British forces and Mohawk allies under Charles de Salaberry repulsed an American attempt to invade Canada.
A group of Russian explorers led by Baron von Toll left their camp on Bennett Island and disappeared without a trace.
The Saint Petersburg Soviet held its first meeting, becoming the first elected body in Russia to represent workers.
Following protests against military leader Robert Guéï, Laurent Gbagbo became the president of Ivory Coast.

links.title: List of heads of state of Ivory Coast

facts.text: Liberian president Edward James Roye was overthrown in modern Africa's first coup d'état.
Ida B. Wells began publishing her research on lynching in the United States, for which she was posthumously awarded a Pulitzer Prize in 2020.

image.caption: Born Ida Bell Wells ( 1862-07-16 ) July 16, 1862 Holly Springs, Mississippi , C.S.

facts.text: Ngô Đình Diệm proclaimed himself president of the newly created Republic of Vietnam after defeating former emperor Bảo Đại in a fraudulent referendum supervised by his brother Ngô Đình Nhu.
Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, considered one of the best video games ever made, in North America.

links.title: List of video games considered the best

facts.text: Somali hospital cook Ali Maow Maalin began displaying symptoms of smallpox, becoming the last person known to be naturally infected by the disease.

Israel and Jordan signed a peace treaty, settling relations between the two countries and pledging that neither would allow its territory to become a staging ground for military strikes by a third country.
Charles V was crowned as Holy Roman Emperor.
The Football Association, world's first governing body of association football, was founded in London.
The Illinois Memorial, honoring Union army soldiers from Illinois who fought at the Siege of Vicksburg, was dedicated at Vicksburg National Military Park.
The Chicago Theatre, the oldest surviving grand movie palace, opened.
President George W. Bush signed the Patriot Act into law, significantly expanding the authority of United States law enforcement agencies.
Franco-Dutch War: French forces surrender the fortress town of Grave to the Dutch army after a three month siege.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of Ich will den Kreuzstab gerne tragen, BWV 56, one of few works he called a cantata.

links.title: Ich will den Kreuzstab gerne tragen, BWV 56

facts.text: Actor Ronald Reagan delivered a speech on behalf of Republican presidential candidate Barry Goldwater, launching his own political career, which culminated in him serving two full terms as U.S. president.
The Boston Red Sox completed a sweep of the St. Louis Cardinals to win the 2004 World Series, breaking the so-called " Curse of the Bambino ".
The Mocking of Christ by Cimabue sold at auction in France for €19.5 million, a record for a pre-1500 artwork.
The first underground segment of the New York City Subway opened, connecting New York City Hall with Harlem.

links.title: Early history of the IRT subway

facts.text: World War I: The Royal Navy dreadnought HMS Audacious was sunk by a mine, but its loss was kept secret for four years.
Inter-religious riots in which Hindu mobs targeted Muslim families began in the Indian state of Bihar, resulting in 2,000 to 30,000 deaths.
American Catholic priest Philip Berrigan led a protest against the Vietnam War by pouring blood over Selective Service records in Baltimore, Maryland.
Widerøe Flight 744 suffered a controlled flight into terrain while on approach to Namsos Airport, Norway, killing two crew members and four passengers.
Armed men led by Nairi Hunanyan carried out a mass shooting at the Armenian parliament, killing Prime Minister Vazgen Sargsyan, National Assembly speaker Karen Demirchyan, and six others.

image.caption: Location National Assembly Building , Yerevan , Armenia

facts.text: King George III expanded on his Proclamation of Rebellion in the Thirteen Colonies in his speech from the throne at the opening of Parliament.
The Empire of Japan achieved a pyrrhic victory against the United States at the Battle of the Santa Cruz Islands.

links.title: Battle of the Santa Cruz Islands

facts.text: U.S. Navy Petty Officer Allen R. Schindler Jr. was killed in Sasebo, Japan, for being gay, which led to the U.S. Armed Forces' " don't ask, don't tell " policy.

links.title: Murder of Allen R. Schindler Jr.

facts.text: Michael D. Higgins was elected President of Ireland with far more votes than any politician in the country's history.
Thai businessman and Leicester City owner Vichai Srivaddhanaprabha along with four others were killed in a helicopter crash near the King Power Stadium in Leicester, England.
The Treaty of Ripon was agreed, ending the Second Bishops' War and forcing Charles I to summon the Long Parliament, ultimately leading to the First English Civil War.
In the first major engagement of the Texas Revolution, the Texian Army repelled a Mexican attack at the grounds of Mission Concepcion south of Downtown San Antonio.
The funerary mask of Tutankhamun, possibly originally made for Queen Neferneferuaten, was uncovered for the first time in approximately 3,250 years.
World War II: Italy invaded Greece after Greek prime minister Ioannis Metaxas rejected Benito Mussolini 's ultimatum demanding the cession of Greek territory.
In St. Louis, Missouri, U.S., the 630-foot (190 m)-tall steel catenary Gateway Arch was completed.
The Hōei earthquake ruptured all segments of the Nankai megathrust simultaneously – the only earthquake recorded to have done so.
American Revolutionary War: As George Washington 's Continental Army retreated northward from New York City, the British Army captured the village of White Plains.
The U.S. Congress passed the Volstead Act over president Woodrow Wilson 's veto, reinforcing Prohibition in the United States.
Indonesian composer Wage Rudolf Supratman introduced " Indonesia Raya ", now the country's national anthem.
Prospero, the first British satellite launched on a British rocket, lifted off from Launch Area 5B in Woomera, South Australia.
Hans-Adam II threatened to dismiss the Landtag of Liechtenstein over disagreements on the date of a referendum for the country's accession to the EEA.
In the Argentine general election, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner became the first woman to be elected president of Argentina.
Civil wars of the Tetrarchy: Constantine the Great defeated Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in Rome.
Ladislaus the Posthumous was crowned King of Bohemia, although George of Poděbrady remained in control of the government.
The Duke of York and Albany 's Maritime Regiment of Foot, the forerunner to the Royal Marines, was established at the grounds of the Honourable Artillery Company in London.
In New York Harbor, U.S. president Grover Cleveland dedicated the Statue of Liberty, a gift from France commemorating the Declaration of Independence.

image.caption: Interactive map of Statue of Liberty Liberty Enlightening the World

facts.text: The first terrorist attack in Beijing's recent history took place when members of the Turkistan Islamic Party drove a vehicle into a crowd, killing five people and injuring thirty-eight others.
William Robert Broughton, a member of George Vancouver 's expedition, observed a peak in the present-day U.S. state of Oregon and named it Mount Hood after British admiral Samuel Hood.
Rioting broke out in Bristol, England, after the Second Reform Bill failed to pass parliament, causing 250 casualties and £300,000 of damage.
American Civil War: The Battle of Wauhatchie, one of the few night battles of the war, concluded with the Union Army opening a supply line to troops in Chattanooga, Tennessee.
The Nanbu clan of Honshu surrendered to imperial forces during the Boshin War.
Israeli Border Police massacred 48 Arab citizens of Kafr Qasim, among them women and children who were returning from work.
Following the nationalisation of the Egypt's Suez Canal, Israel, France, and the United Kingdom invaded the Sinai Peninsula.
A C-46 airliner carrying the Cal Poly Mustangs football team crashed during takeoff from Toledo Express Airport in Ohio, U.S., resulting in 22 deaths.

links.title: California Polytechnic State University football team plane crash

facts.text: Singaporean leftist opposition leader Chia Thye Poh was detained under the Internal Security Act, which allows for preventive detention, and held for 32 years.
British prime minister Margaret Thatcher officially opened the M25, one of Britain's busiest motorways.
Galileo became the first spacecraft to visit an asteroid when it made a flyby of 951 Gaspra.
At 77 years old, former astronaut John Glenn returned to space aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on the STS-95 mission.
Hurricane Sandy, the largest Atlantic hurricane on record, made landfall in New Jersey and caused nearly $75 billion in damages, becoming the second-most destructive storm in U.S. history.
The first phase of the Marmaray project opened with an undersea rail tunnel across the Bosphorus strait.
The San Francisco Mint signed a contract to produce the Kalākaua coinage for the Hawaiian Kingdom.
Arab–Israeli War: The Israel Defense Forces massacred at least 52 villagers while capturing the Palestinian Arab village of Safsaf.
An explosion, likely caused by a World War II–era naval mine, capsized the Soviet ship Novorossiysk in the harbor of Sevastopol, with the loss of 608 men.
About 10,000 people died when the most intense tropical cyclone ever recorded in the North Indian Ocean made landfall in the Indian state of Odisha near Bhubaneswar.
Somali pirates hijacked a North Korean ship in the Indian Ocean northeast of Mogadishu.
War of the Fourth Coalition: Believing that they were outnumbered, the German garrison at Stettin surrendered to a much smaller French force without a fight.
Seventeen-year-old Vilhelm, Prince of Denmark, arrived in Athens to become King George I of Greece.
CBS Radio broadcast " The War of the Worlds ", a radio drama that newspapers accused of tricking Americans into believing there was an actual Martian invasion.

links.title: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)

facts.text: A luzzu (Maltese fishing boat) overloaded with passengers capsized and sank in the Gozo Channel off Qala, killing 23 of the 27 people on board.

A squad of 120 North Korean Army commandos landed in boats along a 25-mile long section of the eastern coast of South Korea in a failed attempt to overthrow the dictatorship of Park Chung Hee and reunify Korea.
As the military dictatorship came to an end, Argentina's first democratic election in a decade resulted in Raúl Alfonsín being elected president.
The Madrid Conference, an attempt by the international community to revive the Israeli–Palestinian peace process through negotiations, convened.
The Troubles: Three members of the Ulster Defence Association opened fire in a crowded pub during a Halloween party, killing eight people and wounding nineteen others.
After his terminal-cancer diagnosis, Warren Zevon made his last public appearance on the Late Show with David Letterman, giving the advice to "enjoy every sandwich".

links.title: Warren Zevon on the Late Show with David Letterman in 2002

facts.text: Lobengula, King of Matabeleland, granted the Rudd Concession to agents of Cecil Rhodes, leading to the creation of the British South Africa Company.
At the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Michael Woodruff performed the first successful kidney transplantation in the United Kingdom.

English model Jean Shrimpton wore a controversially short minidress to Derby Day at Flemington Racecourse in Melbourne, Australia – a pivotal moment of the introduction of the miniskirt to women's fashion.

links.title: White shift dress of Jean Shrimpton

facts.text: American comedians Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert hosted the Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear in Washington, D.C.

links.title: Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear

facts.text: A magnitude-7.0 earthquake occurred in the Aegean Sea between Greece and Turkey, triggering a tsunami and causing 119 deaths.
World War I: Allied forces defeated Turkish troops in Beersheba in Southern Palestine at the Battle of Beersheba, with the battle involving one of the last successful cavalry charges.
100 crew members of the USS Reuben James perished when their vessel became the first U.S. Navy ship sunk by hostile action during World War II after it was torpedoed by the German submarine U-552.
A gas explosion at the Indiana State Fairgrounds Coliseum in Indianapolis killed 81 people and injured about 400 others.

links.title: 1963 Indiana State Fairgrounds Coliseum gas explosion

facts.text: Three Provisional Irish Republican Army members escaped from Mountjoy Prison in Dublin aboard a hijacked helicopter that landed in the prison's exercise yard.
TG4, the world's first Irish language television station, began broadcasting.
After 22 years in power, Mahathir Mohamad retired as Prime Minister of Malaysia.
Public-transportation workers in Indianapolis went on strike, shutting down mass transit in the city.
Approximately 400 workers completed the 60-foot ( 18 m ) busts of U.S. presidents George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln at Mount Rushmore in South Dakota.
Indian prime minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two of her own Sikh bodyguards, sparking riots that killed thousands of Sikhs.
All 217 people on board EgyptAir Flight 990 perished when the aircraft suddenly crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts.
The discovery of the Plutonian moons Nix and Hydra, based on photographs taken by the Hubble Space Telescope nearly five months prior, was announced.
Romulus Augustulus took the throne as the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire.
Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses onto the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg, marking the beginning of the Protestant Reformation.
Australian sailor Jesse Martin arrived in Melbourne, becoming the youngest person to circumnavigate the globe solo, non-stop, and unassisted.

links.title: List of youth solo sailing circumnavigations

facts.text: Singapore Airlines Flight 006 collided with construction equipment while attempting to take off from Chiang Kai-shek International Airport in Taiwan during heavy rain, killing 83 people aboard.
An Uzbek immigrant drove a rented truck into cyclists and runners in Lower Manhattan, New York City, killing eight people.
